summary: DNS is defined across dozens of RFCs, and its terminology has shifted over decades. This document gives current definitions for many DNS terms in one place. It updates RFC 2308 by clarifying "forwarder" and "QNAME", and it replaces RFC 8499 with added terms and clarifications.

plainLanguage.summary: DNS is described across dozens of RFCs, and its words have changed meaning over the years. This document gives the current meaning of many DNS terms in one place, so that people can agree on what they are saying.

subtitle: One place to look up what DNS terms mean today, from labels and zones to resolvers and DNSSEC states.

tldr.problem: The DNS is defined across dozens of RFCs, and many of its terms have drifted from their original meanings or were never defined precisely.
tldr.mechanism: The document collects current definitions in one place, grouped by topic: names, response codes, resource records, servers, zones, wildcards, registration and DNSSEC. It quotes the source RFC where the consensus matches, and gives a new stand-alone definition where it does not.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice that obsoletes RFC 8499 and updates RFC 2308 by clarifying forwarder and QNAME. It is a reference to skip around in, not a tutorial.

today: RFC 9499 is a Best Current Practice, numbered BCP 219, and was published in March 2024. It obsoletes RFC 8499 and updates RFC 2308 by clarifying the definitions of forwarder and QNAME. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why a DNS Dictionary Exists
sections.content:
The Domain Name System is a simple query-response protocol whose messages have the same format in both directions. The protocol and the message format come from RFC 1034 and RFC 1035, and later documents defined more terms. Some of those early terms now mean something a little different than they did in 1987.

This document collects a wide variety of DNS terms, organized loosely by topic. Some were defined precisely in an earlier RFC, some loosely, and some not at all. Where the community consensus matches an earlier RFC, that RFC is quoted. Where the consensus has moved on, the RFC is mentioned and a new stand-alone definition is given. Appendix A lists the definitions this document updates, and Appendix B the ones it defines for the first time.

The RFC says outright that there is no single consistent definition of the DNS. It can mean a naming scheme for objects on the Internet, a distributed database of names and their properties, an architecture for maintaining that database, or the query-response protocol that implements it. To deal with this the document defines the global DNS and the private DNS.

Readers are warned that the terms are grouped by topic, and that someone new to the DNS probably cannot learn it from front to back here. Skipping around, with the help of the index, is the intended way to read it. The words byte and octet are used interchangeably.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a reference work, not a tutorial. The RFC says a reader new to DNS should use the index and look up one term at a time.

sections.title: Names, Labels and Formats
sections.content:
A domain name is an ordered list of one or more labels, and a label is an ordered list of zero or more octets. The global DNS is described with a short list of facets of any naming system: how names are composed, their format, who administers them, what data they carry, what metadata they have, which protocol fetches the data, and the context for resolving them. The private DNS uses the same protocol but does not rely on the global DNS root zone.

In the global DNS each label is between 0 and 63 octets long, and the last label of a fully qualified name is the zero-length root label. A name has a maximum total length of 255 octets in wire format. Names appear in three formats: wire format, where each label is preceded by a length octet; presentation format, where labels are separated by dots and a fully qualified name ends with the root dot, as in example.tld.; and common display format, which is the same but usually leaves the root dot off.

The section also untangles several loose terms. A fully qualified domain name is often written without the terminating dot. Host name is not defined in the core DNS RFCs and usually means a name that follows the preferred name syntax. A top-level domain is a zone one layer below the root, such as com or jp, and the RFC says there is nothing special about top-level domains from the point of view of the DNS. Other entries cover multicast DNS, locally served zones, subdomains, aliases and the canonical name.
sections.plainLanguage: A domain name lists its parts from the smallest to the largest. Each part is a label, and the last label is empty because it stands for the root of the whole system.

sections.title: Response Codes and the QNAME
sections.content:
Several response codes from RFC 1035 have shorthand names: NOERROR, FORMERR, SERVFAIL, NXDOMAIN, NOTIMP and REFUSED. NODATA is a pseudo response code: the name is valid but there are no records of the requested type, shown as NOERROR with no relevant answers in the Answer section. The RFC notes that calling it NXRRSET is a mistake, because that name belongs to a specific error code in RFC 2136.

The header of a DNS message is its first 12 octets. The term QNAME had two meanings: the name in the Question section of a query, or, in RFC 2308, the name in the answer after following a CNAME chain. To remove the confusion the RFC distinguishes QNAME (original), QNAME (effective) and QNAME (final), and notes that in general use QNAME almost always means the original one.

A referral is a response in which a server that is not completely authoritative points the resolver to another place to send its query. A downward referral, from a server authoritative for part of the QNAME, is what normal operation needs in order to find names beneath a delegation. An upward referral, usually pointing at the root, is never required, and some people regard it as a misconfiguration. A response with only a referral has an empty Answer section, the NS RRset in the Authority section, and the AA bit clear.
sections.plainLanguage: A resolver that cannot answer sends the client on to another server. That hand-off is a referral, and a downward referral is the normal way to walk down the DNS tree.

sections.title: Records, RRsets and TTL
sections.content:
An RR is a resource record. An RRset is a set of records with the same owner name, class and type but different data, and RFC 2181 requires the TTLs of all records in an RRset to be the same. RRSIG records are the exception: they are tied to the RRset they sign and do not form RRsets themselves.

The TTL is the maximum time a record may be cached. It is an unsigned number with a minimum of 0 and a maximum of 2147483647, encoded in the less significant 31 bits of the 32-bit field. It is a maximum because a cache operator may shorten it, for example under a policy against large values. The RFC also notes that some servers are known to ignore TTLs on some RRsets, against the advice in RFC 1035.

Other entries define the master file (zone file) and the presentation format, EDNS, which allows message sizes larger than the original 512-octet limit, a bigger response code space and extra options, the OPT pseudo-record, the SOA field names (MNAME, RNAME, SERIAL, REFRESH, RETRY, EXPIRE, MINIMUM), and address records of type A and AAAA.
sections.plainLanguage: Each record carries a time to live, which is the longest a cache may keep it. A cache may shorten that time, and the RFC notes that some servers ignore the value altogether.

sections.title: Resolvers, Servers and Transports
sections.content:
Terms such as DNS server and name server have no formal definition and need context. A resolver extracts information from name servers on behalf of clients. A stub resolver cannot perform all resolution itself and depends on a recursive resolver, which acts in recursive mode: it answers from its cache or queries other servers for the final answer. A recursive query has the RD bit set to 1 and a non-recursive query has it set to 0. In iterative resolution the client repeatedly makes non-recursive queries and follows referrals.

An authoritative server knows the content of a zone from local knowledge and answers with the AA flag set. The primary and secondary roles describe which server is the source of zone transfers, where AXFR copies the full zone and IXFR only the parts that changed; the RFC notes that current usage has moved from master and slave to primary and secondary. A forwarder is a server used to resolve queries instead of directly using the authoritative nameserver chain, and in current use forwarders often sit between stub resolvers and recursive servers. Priming is the act of finding the list of root servers from a configuration, and the root hints file is used for it.

The section also defines policy-implementing and open resolvers, split DNS and views, passive DNS, anycast, and the transports: Classic DNS over UDP or TCP, which is not encrypted, DNS-over-TLS, DNS-over-HTTPS and DNS-over-QUIC, plus zone transfers over TLS.
sections.plainLanguage: The section names the roles in a lookup. A stub resolver only asks, a recursive resolver does the asking, and an authoritative server answers from what it already knows.

sections.title: Zones, Delegation and Glue
sections.content:
A zone is a unit of authoritative information. The apex (or origin) is the name at the top of a zone, and a zone cut separates a parent zone from a child zone. Delegation happens when an NS RRset is added in the parent zone for the child origin. Glue records are address records for name servers that are only needed when the server's name is below the cut, so that the NS records do not send you to the very address you are trying to learn.

Following RFC 9471, the relationship between the NS owner name, the name server name and the zone origin is one of three types: unrelated, in-domain, or sibling domain. The RFC gives a table, for example example.org with ns.example.org as in-domain and ns.ietf.org as sibling domain. The terms lame delegation and bailiwick are described as having drifted or as confusing, and are to be considered historic.

Wildcards, which are records owned by a name starting with the asterisk label, are treated in their own section, including the closest encloser and the source of synthesis. The registration model defines registry, registrant, registrar, EPP, WHOIS, RDAP, DNS operator and public suffix, noting that whoever decides what goes into a zone is its registry.
sections.plainLanguage: A delegation hands part of a namespace to another party. The parent zone keeps a pointer to the child's name servers, and glue holds their addresses when those names cannot be resolved on their own.

sections.title: The Four DNSSEC States
sections.content:
A validating resolver can place a response in one of four states: secure, insecure, bogus or indeterminate. The states are defined in RFC 4033 and RFC 4035, and the two documents word them differently. This document quotes both and takes no position on whether they need to be reconciled.

The rest of the DNSSEC section names the parts. A signed zone has signed RRsets and properly built DNSKEY, RRSIG, NSEC (or NSEC3) and optionally DS records. NSEC and NSEC3 provide authenticated denial of existence, and NSEC3 mitigates zone enumeration and supports Opt-Out. Validation can mean checking signatures, checking responses such as a denial of existence, or building an authentication chain from a trust anchor to a response.

The key terms are the key signing key, which signs only the apex DNSKEY RRset, the zone signing key, which signs the other RRsets, and the combined signing key, which does both. The RFC stresses that operational practice, not the protocol, decides which role a key plays, and that the SEP flag is only a hint.
sections.plainLanguage: DNSSEC signs DNS data so a checker can tell a real answer from a forged one. This part names the keys and lists the four verdicts a checker can reach.

sections.title: Security and IANA Notes
sections.content:
The security section is one sentence: these definitions do not change any security considerations for either the global DNS or private DNS. The IANA section records that references to RFC 8499 in the IANA registries have been replaced with references to this document.

Because the document only defines words, the practical risk is misunderstanding rather than a new attack. Using the agreed meanings, for example for a validating resolver or a lame delegation, is how the community avoids talking past each other.
sections.plainLanguage: The document changes no security rules. Its value is that everyone uses the same words, so a sentence about DNS means the same thing to every reader.

viz.caption: COMMON DNS RESPONSE CODES AND WHAT THEY MEAN

items.title: NOERROR
items.text: No error condition. The query was understood and processed.

items.title: NXDOMAIN
items.text: Name Error. The domain name in the query does not exist.

items.title: SERVFAIL
items.text: Server failure. The name server could not process the query because of a problem with the server.

items.title: REFUSED
items.text: The name server refuses to perform the operation, usually for policy reasons.

items.title: NODATA
items.text: A pseudo code. The name is valid but there are no records of the requested type, so the answer is NOERROR with no relevant answers.

viz.caption: RECURSIVE AND ITERATIVE RESOLUTION, AS DESCRIBED IN RFC 1034

left.title: Recursive
left.desc: The server pursues the query on the client's behalf and returns either an answer or an error, but never a referral.

right.title: Iterative
right.desc: The server refers the client to another server and lets the client pursue the query there.

viz.caption: DELEGATION TYPES FROM TABLE 1 OF THE RFC
THE FOUR DNSSEC STATES AS WORDED IN RFC 4033 AND RFC 4035

cells: The resolver has a trust anchor, has a chain of trust, and can verify all the signatures in the response.
The resolver can build a chain of signed DNSKEY and DS records from a trusted anchor to the RRset.
There is signed proof that no DS record exists at some delegation point, so later branches are provably insecure.
The resolver knows there is no chain of signed DNSKEY and DS records to the RRset, for example in an unsigned zone.
A secure delegation says the data is signed but the response fails to validate, for example because signatures are missing or expired.
The resolver believes it should be able to build a chain of trust but cannot, because signatures fail or data is missing.
No trust anchor indicates that this part of the tree is secure. This is the default mode.
The resolver cannot tell whether the RRset should be signed, because it cannot obtain the needed DNSSEC records.
